record.notes: US State Department Indonesia advisory opened 2026-10-13; advisory issued 2026-07-07. Indonesian Immigration guidance should also be checked directly before departure. Review after 2026-11-13.

record.value: Check the passport used to enter is also used to leave Indonesia. Keep visa approval, payment receipt, onward ticket, accommodation details and arrival-declaration QR confirmation accessible. The arrival declaration, visa, Bali tourist levy and customs declaration are distinct requirements or charges and should not be conflated. For travel with medication, verify each active ingredient with Indonesian authorities; a US prescription does not automatically authorize import.
Carry a copy of the passport as proof of identity and visa status (State Dept).
All travelers must complete the All Indonesia arrival declaration (immigration, customs, health, quarantine) online within 3 days before arrival. The form is free.

Use a combination of Indonesian rupiah cash and cards. Cash remains useful for small vendors, markets, local transport and smaller businesses; card acceptance is more common at established hotels and larger restaurants. Confirm fees and acceptance with the specific merchant.
Cash still needed for small vendors, drivers, entrance fees and many warungs; cards widely taken at hotels, larger restaurants and shops, often with a surcharge
record.notes: Not opened at a primary source today. General pattern; the surcharge practice needs a source before a percentage is stated.

record.value: Cash is widely used for small purchases, local warungs, and markets. Cards (Visa/Mastercard) are accepted at hotels, mid-range to upscale restaurants, and larger shops. QR code payments (QRIS) are common but generally require an Indonesian bank account or e-wallet; foreign cards and apps typically cannot use QRIS directly.

ATMs are available in major visitor areas but reliability, withdrawal limits, fees and machine security vary. Use bank-affiliated machines in secure locations and decline dynamic currency conversion when it offers a clearly unfavorable rate.
ATMs are common in south Bali and Ubud and sparse on the Nusa islands and in the north/east
record.notes: Not opened at a primary source today. Per-transaction limits and operator fees appear in secondary results with inconsistent figures - leave figures out until sourced.

record.value: ATMs are widely available in tourist areas (Kuta, Seminyak, Ubud, Sanur). Withdrawal limits are typically IDR 2,500,000–3,000,000 per transaction. Foreign card fees apply. Use ATMs inside banks or major convenience stores to reduce skimming risk.

The US State Department reports a maximum of IDR 100000000 for currency on entry and exit and notes that currency at or above the declaration threshold must be declared. Customs says cash and/or payment instruments totaling IDR 100000000 or more must be declared. Do not treat the stated maximum as permission to evade a declaration requirement.
record.notes: Opened 2026-10-13. Primary customs page: https://ecd.beacukai.go.id/forms/bc22 . Customs page says declaration is required at IDR 100000000 or more; the State Department describes a maximum of IDR 100000000 on entry and exit. Preserve this wording difference and check current Indonesian rules before travel.

record.value: Not a cap but a DECLARATION duty: cash and/or other payment instruments worth at least IDR 100,000,000 (rupiah or foreign equivalent) must be declared to Customs on entry or exit. Taking IDR 100,000,000 or more in rupiah OUT also needs a Bank Indonesia permit; bringing that much rupiah IN must be declared and checked for authenticity. An individual may not carry foreign banknotes worth IDR 1,000,000,000 or more. Not declaring: administrative penalty of 10% of the amount carried, capped at IDR 300,000,000
record.notes: Indonesian Customs FAQ citing PMK 100/PMK.04/2018. RESOLVES the panel dispute: the State Dept page's 'Entry maximum / Exit maximum: 100,000,000 rupiah' is a simplification; chatgpt and deepseek read it correctly as a declaration threshold. Never print the State Dept's dollar equivalent.

record.value: IDR 100,000,000 (approximately USD 5,600) or equivalent in foreign currency must be declared. Amounts exceeding this require a customs declaration.
record.notes: Confirm current threshold with Indonesian Customs (beacukai.go.id) before travel.

record.value: Tipping is discretionary rather than universally mandatory. Check whether a service charge is already included; a small additional tip may be appropriate for good service. Norms vary by service, venue and local practice.
Not obligatory. Many restaurant and hotel bills already add service and tax; small tips for drivers, guides and spa staff are customary
record.notes: Not opened at a primary source today. The service/tax percentages must be sourced before being stated.

record.value: Tipping is not mandatory but appreciated. Many hotels and restaurants add a 5–10% service charge and 10% government tax. If a service charge is already included, additional tipping is optional. For private drivers, IDR 50,000–100,000 per day is customary. For spa therapists, IDR 20,000–50,000 is common.

record.value: Bali has no intercity passenger rail network. Trains can be useful on Java, but reaching Bali from Java requires a road-and-ferry connection or a flight.
None on Bali
No intercity rail on Bali. Indonesia has limited rail on Java (Jakarta–Surabaya) but it does not connect to Bali.

Bali has public buses and shuttle services, but coverage and frequency do not make them a universal substitute for private transport. Check the specific route, stop and operating schedule before planning around a bus.
Limited public and tourist shuttle services; not a practical backbone for a short trip
record.notes: Not opened at a primary source today.

record.value: Public buses (Trans Metro Dewata) exist in Denpasar and surrounding areas but are not practical for most tourist itineraries. Private shuttles and minivans (Perama, Kura-Kura) connect major tourist areas (Kuta, Ubud, Padang Bai, Amed).
Domestic flights connect Bali with major Indonesian destinations. Airlines, schedules, baggage allowances and change fees vary; check the operating airline's rules for the actual fare.
DPS has domestic links, including to Lombok and to Labuan Bajo for Komodo
record.notes: Not opened at a primary source today. Baggage allowances and change fees vary by carrier and fare; secondary figures seen were inconsistent.

record.value: Domestic flights connect DPS to Jakarta (CGK), Surabaya (SUB), Yogyakarta (YIA), Lombok (LOP), and other Indonesian cities. Garuda Indonesia, Lion Air, Citilink, and Batik Air operate these routes. Baggage allowances are typically 20 kg checked plus 7 kg carry-on; low-cost carriers charge for checked bags.

Grab and Gojek operate in parts of Bali, with availability and pickup rules varying by location. Some tourist attractions, ports and locally regulated areas can complicate pickups. Confirm availability in the app and agree on a lawful pickup point.
Grab and Gojek operate; licensed taxis are widely available and Blue Bird is described as generally the most reliable
record.notes: State Dept wording covers 'major Indonesian cities'. The Bali-specific pickup restrictions (airport, parts of Ubud and the Bukit) come from secondary sources only and are unverified.

record.value: Grab and Gojek are the dominant ride-hailing apps. They operate widely in Bali but are banned in certain areas (e.g., some traditional markets, parts of Ubud, and certain beach areas) to protect local transport cooperatives. In banned zones, you must walk to a designated pickup point or use a local taxi.

Indonesia drives on the left. Foreign visitors should verify their license, applicable international driving permit and motorcycle-specific entitlement before driving. Scooter rental does not confer legal permission to ride. Insurance exclusions, road conditions, congestion and local enforcement are material risks. No current official blood-alcohol limit or detailed licensing rule was verified in this research pass.
record.notes: US State Department advisory opened 2026-10-13. Verify licensing and insurance directly before publication.

record.value: A US licence alone is not recognized; foreign drivers must carry an International Driving Permit. Helmets are mandatory on motorcycles. Carry ID and vehicle registration. After an accident, stay and notify police. If fined, ask for an official receipt
record.notes: Driving is on the left (stable). Whether a US car-only licence plus IDP covers a scooter - the motorcycle-endorsement question - was NOT answered on the page and is the crux of two articles. BLOOD-ALCOHOL: deepseek alone gave limits (0.0% under 21, 0.05% otherwise); no primary source was found for any numeric limit, and a search surfaced an Indonesian law-journal comparison stating Indonesia has no BAC standard (the traffic law punishes driving without full concentration). Treat deepseek's figures as unsupported - do not publish. MOTORCYCLE ENDORSEMENT: still no primary source. Secondary Bali sites say the permit must carry the motorcycle category and name the 1968 convention; US-issued permits are a point to check specifically, since that is exactly what an American would hold. The police pages found concern Indonesians obtaining an international licence, not inbound visitors. US-ISSUED PERMIT: the AAA country list (https://cluballiance.aaa.com/travel/idp/international-drivers-permit-countries, opened 2026-10-13) lists 'Indonesia*' with the footnote 'Not party to 1949 Convention: International Driving Permit Honored' - so the AAA permit an American would carry is honored. The page says nothing about vehicle categories; the motorcycle-category requirement is still supported only by secondary Bali sites, one of which names the 1968 convention (in tension with the AAA note).

record.value: Driving is on the left side of the road. A valid US driver's license alone is not sufficient for renting a car or scooter; an International Driving Permit (IDP) with the appropriate class (motorcycle endorsement for scooters) is required. Police checks are common. BAC limit is 0.0% for drivers under 21; for others, the legal limit is 0.05%.
record.notes: Driving side: left. IDP requirement: must correspond to the vehicle class (car vs. motorcycle). Helmets are mandatory for scooters. BAC: 0.05% for drivers 21+; zero tolerance for under 21. Verify current enforcement and insurance requirements.

record.value: Bali generally has a wetter period around November through March and a relatively drier period around April through October, but timing varies by year, altitude and locality. Rain can occur during the nominal dry season; monthly climate descriptions are not daily forecasts. Check BMKG's current regional seasonal forecast.
record.notes: BMKG Bali's climatology service was available and showed seasonal bulletins; the page retrieved for this pass included an older 2025 forecast, not a verified forecast for the complete 2026-27 travel season. Do not present its 2025 dates as current.

record.value: Tropical: a drier season roughly April-October and a wetter season roughly November-March; warm all year
record.notes: Month boundaries vary by year; use ranges. Rainfall figures need the meteorological agency (BMKG) before any number is printed.

record.value: Tropical climate with two main seasons: Dry season (April/May–October) with sunny days, lower humidity, and calmer seas. Rainy season (November–March) with frequent afternoon downpours, higher humidity, and occasional strong winds. Temperatures average 26–30°C (79–86°F) year-round.

US Department of State: Level 2, Exercise Increased Caution for Indonesia. Advisory issued 2026-07-07. It cites natural disasters, unrest and terrorism; the advisory specifically says not to travel to Central Papua and Highland Papua. These restrictions are not a statement that Bali itself is under a blanket do-not-travel warning.
record.notes: Official US government advisory opened 2026-10-13; displayed issue date 2026-07-07. Review after 2026-10-20 because advisories can change. Check the page again before every trip.

record.value: Level 2 - Exercise increased caution (natural disasters, unrest, terrorism); Level 4 Do Not Travel applies only to Central Papua and Highland Papua
record.notes: Advisory 'Date issued: July 07, 2026' at the top of the page; the travel-guidance block shows 'Date issued: July 09, 2026'. Both dates are on the page - cite the advisory date and re-check.

record.notes: Level 2 due to natural disasters, unrest, and terrorism. Do not travel to Central Papua and Highland Papua (Level 4). Bali is not under a 'do not travel' advisory.

record.value: Road crashes, especially involving motorcycles; mosquito-borne illness; gastrointestinal illness; ocean currents and drowning; volcanic activity, earthquakes and other natural hazards; theft and scams; alcohol adulteration; and severe legal consequences for prohibited drugs. Risk varies substantially by activity and location.
Road traffic, especially scooters
record.notes: Not opened at a primary source today. Widely reported; needs a citable source before being ranked as 'the main' risk.

record.value: Natural disasters (earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, tsunamis), terrorism (low but present), demonstrations that can turn violent, and road safety (scooter accidents are a leading cause of injury for tourists).

Consult a travel-health clinician at least a month before departure. CDC recommends routine vaccines be up to date and recommends hepatitis A for unvaccinated travelers aged one year or older and hepatitis B for unvaccinated travelers of all ages. Typhoid is recommended for most travelers. Rabies pre-exposure vaccination depends on exposure and access to prompt care. Japanese encephalitis vaccination depends on itinerary and duration. CDC reported Zika cases in returning travelers from Bali in a notice dated 2026-08-07; mosquito and sexual-transmission precautions are important, and pregnancy-related travel advice needs particular care.
record.notes: Official CDC traveler page opened 2026-10-13. Its retrieved content identifies the Zika notice dated 2026-08-07 and vaccine guidance. Review after 2026-10-20 and again before publication. Recommendations depend on health history, route and duration.

record.value: None required for entry (State Dept). CDC recommends hepatitis A, hepatitis B and typhoid for most travelers, routine vaccines up to date, Japanese encephalitis for longer or higher-risk stays, and a pre-exposure rabies discussion
record.notes: Entry requirement from https://travel.state.gov/en/international-travel/travel-advisories/indonesia.html

record.value: No vaccines are mandatory for US citizens arriving directly from the US. CDC recommends routine vaccines (MMR, Tdap, polio, influenza) plus hepatitis A, typhoid, and rabies (for certain travelers). Yellow fever vaccine is required only if arriving from a country with yellow fever transmission. COVID-19 vaccination is no longer required.
record.notes: Consult CDC Travelers' Health page for Indonesia before travel. Rabies pre-exposure vaccination is recommended for those who may be exposed to animals (monkeys, dogs).

record.value: Do not assume tap water is potable. Travelers generally use sealed bottled water or water treated by a reliable provider for drinking; ice and food hygiene require judgment. Avoid claiming that all water or ice in every establishment is unsafe or safe.
Not treated as drinkable; use bottled or filtered water
record.notes: Not opened at a primary source today. CDC says follow safe food and water practices; a Bali-specific statement was not read.
Tap water in Bali is not safe to drink. Use bottled or filtered water for drinking and brushing teeth. Ice in reputable establishments is typically made from purified water.

value.ambulance: 118 or 119; availability and dispatch arrangements can vary

record.notes: Numbers are commonly published for Indonesia but were not confirmed against a currently opened official emergency-services directory during this pass. Verify before publishing and include local hospital and insurer emergency contacts.

Badung regency (the regency covering Kuta, Seminyak, Canggu, Jimbaran and the Bukit) communications office: 'Kepolisian = 110, Pemadam Kebakaran = 113, Basarnas = 115, Ambulan/Kemenkes = 119', with 112 as the free unified number. The national 112 page (https://layanan112.komdigi.go.id/tentang) confirms 112 is a single free emergency number run by local governments and reachable without credit. Panel note: chatgpt and deepseek both gave 'ambulance 118 or 119'; 118 was seen only in Google result snippets from other regional government sites, not opened.
General emergency: 112. Bali tourist police: +62-361-759687. Bali provincial police service center (24h): +62-361-222200.

record.value: Travelers can consider an international eSIM, a local Indonesian SIM or roaming. Device compatibility, data allowance, ID registration and whether a foreign handset needs IMEI registration depend on the plan and circumstances. Confirm current tourist registration rules with the carrier and Indonesian authorities; do not state that every short-term visitor must register a foreign handset without verifying the applicable exemption.
Travel eSIMs and local SIMs both work; a local number helps with ride apps
record.notes: Not opened at a primary source today.

record.value: eSIMs from providers like Ubigi, Airalo, and Holafly work in Indonesia and can be purchased before travel. Local prepaid SIM cards (Telkomsel, XL, Indosat) are widely available at airports and convenience stores. Tourists must register a local SIM with their passport; no Indonesian tax ID (NPWP) is required.

Coverage is generally better in developed tourist areas than in remote, mountainous or offshore locations. Coverage on Nusa Penida, Nusa Lembongan, the Gilis and remote parts of Bali varies by carrier and terrain. Download offline maps and retain key bookings offline.
Good in south Bali and Ubud; patchier in the highlands, the north and parts of Nusa Penida
record.notes: Not opened at a primary source today.

record.value: 4G/LTE coverage is good in Bali's tourist areas (Kuta, Seminyak, Ubud, Sanur, Nusa Dua). 5G is available in some areas. Rural and remote areas (north Bali, Nusa Penida interior) may have weaker or spotty coverage.

Beachwear is appropriate at many beaches and pools but not generally suitable for temple visits or formal religious settings. At temples, follow posted rules and staff guidance, cover shoulders and knees as required, and use a sarong where requested. Dress expectations differ between ordinary public spaces and religious ceremonies.
Temples require a sarong and sash and covered shoulders; beachwear stays at the beach
record.notes: Not opened at a primary source today. The provincial government has issued a formal list of rules for foreign visitors; only news reports of it were seen. The current circular itself must be opened for the 'rules for tourists' article.

record.value: Dress modestly at temples: sarong and sash required (usually available for rent or loan at temple entrances). Shoulders and knees should be covered. Beachwear is fine at the beach but not in towns or temples.

value: Respect temple rules, sacred spaces and local directions.
Ask permission before photographing people or ceremonies.
Do not step on or deliberately disturb Balinese daily offerings.
Dress appropriately when entering temples and other religious sites.
Do not touch another person's head or use feet to point at people or sacred objects.
Avoid littering and respect environmental restrictions.
Do not assume that foreign prescriptions, cannabis, CBD or recreational drugs are legal in Indonesia.
Respect Nyepi restrictions and local instructions.
Check the full price and conditions of tours, rentals, boat transfers and accommodation before paying.
do not step on daily offerings when it can be avoided
do not climb on temple structures or sacred trees
keep ceremonies' road closures in mind when timing a drive

value: DO: Use your right hand for giving/receiving, eating, and pointing.
DO: Remove shoes before entering a home or temple.
DON'T: Step on offerings (small palm-leaf trays on the ground).
DON'T: Touch someone's head (considered sacred).
DON'T: Point with your index finger; use your thumb or whole hand.
DON'T: Display affection publicly (holding hands is fine; kissing is not).
DON'T: Raise your voice or show anger; maintain calm and patience.

record.value: Commonly reached by fast boat from Bali, often from Sanur. Boat schedules, ports, sea conditions and operator procedures vary.
Fast boat from Sanur, Padang Bai, or Kusamba to Toya Pakeh or Sampalan (30–45 min). Boats are frequent in the morning but can be cancelled due to rough seas.
Private driver or locally arranged transport is often more practical than assuming easy self-driving. Roads can be rough, narrow and slow, and access to viewpoints may involve steep steps.
Scooter rental is the main way to explore (roads are rough; only for experienced riders). Private drivers with cars are also available for hire.
No commercial airport is normally used for tourist access; boat transfers from Bali are the usual route.
No airport on Nusa Penida; nearest is DPS (Bali)
